Rosa Gattorno's spiritual profile would be incomplete if one left aside her personality as foundress, indeed if the preceding chapters were not, as it were, grafted onto her ecclesial mission and illuminated by her charism.

It is not, however, within the scope of this study to present the exceptional figure of the foundress of the Daughters of Saint Anne in her historical reality, bound up with the origins and vicissitudes of the Institute, which would require a separate volume. I will limit myself to highlighting, in summary form, those aspects in which certain evangelical traits appear in relation to the responsibilities she assumed, by God's will, as guide of the Work. Moreover, several of these aspects have already been illustrated in the various themes treated, since her personal spirituality cannot be separated from her awareness of being foundress.

1. The burden of a mission beyond human measure.

Rosa Gattorno found herself a foundress at the end of an unplanned journey, made under the impulse of charity and in submission to the hierarchical Church; indeed, one may say it was obedience to the diocesan prelate and to the Roman Pontiff that placed her before the hard choice mentioned several times.

Like so many other founders, she was certain that everything was the effect of a plan drawn from on high. It was God, the eternal Father, who guided her steps along unknown and often bewildering paths. This is precisely the interpretation she herself gave, in her book Trials and Consolations, to the vicissitudes of God's Work, of which she considers herself a humble instrument: a toilsome journey through dark forests and frightful precipices, a voyage on a stormy sea to bring the little boat into port; always fearful, yet always sure of the help of her Crucified.

The more her lived awareness of her charism as foundress grows, the more she sinks into her own nothingness and unworthiness, and the more she fears being an obstacle to God's Work. She writes in February 1877:

"If someone does me a kindness, and praise is given to the Institute, and something is attributed to me, horror! I feel torn apart: my nothingness rises so before my eyes that I am as if crushed, and I would throw myself on the ground, as I do at night, weeping. My God! an abyss of infamy is believed good and capable of doing good: it is impossible!

Ah! make everyone know who I am, as you give me the grace to see myself mirrored in such misshapen ugliness. Alas! never allow these poor creatures to be deceived by the outward appearance they see, but make them see what I see of misery and infamy!" (M 4.4, p. 118f).

Deeply convinced as she is that everything is God's work, she naturally attributes to him every success in the presence and action of the Daughters of Saint Anne and the Institute's rapid expansion; whereas each time a difficulty arises or unpleasant news reaches her about the sisters' conduct, she attributes it to her own incapacity or her own faults:

"What am I to say? Only that this happens because of me: here are my sins! Courage, let us trust in God: since it is his Work, he will provide for everything" - "Ah! yes, let me say it: this Work, the blows it receives are all the fruit of my wickedness. If this is what pleases God, let us adore his divine Majesty" (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 6-8-1870, 16-11-1871).

This same awareness that she herself was the real obstacle to the progress of God's Work led her more than once to think of resigning and leaving the responsibility of general government to someone else. But noticing that this thought assailed her precisely at times of great distress over the Work, she suspected it was suggested by the infernal enemy, and so she resisted it as a temptation, as though she were selfishly trying to escape the burden of her mission. On June 5, 1880, when the bishop unjustly accused her of helping her own children with the Institute's goods, she wrote:

"I suffer immensely... I will not say what the enemy is suggesting to me; ah! he takes advantage of it, and so torments me immensely. He goes so far as to say to me: "There will be no more peace for you... Then I keep studying how I might manage to be removed from this office; I study it and this almost comforts me, when I find in my mind a way that seems to me the one that could help me be removed and put in any lowly office. But I no longer pray for this. It is true that I see the traitor, who at once seems to say: I have won!..." (M 4.5, pp. 196-205).

Mother Rosa's charismatic awareness underwent a clarification and, I would say, a progressive growth. Without her realising it, God made her mature through a series of liberations from the constraints that successively prevented her from cooperating fully with the divine plan, in the originality of her own evangelical path.

God led her out of her native Genoa to free her not only from the nearness of her family and relatives but also from the social and religious commitments that bound her to the works and associations of which she had become the soul.

In Piacenza she felt free and available for God's work. But here too she would have to break free of new constraints that could divert the Institute from its purpose or at least hinder its spiritual and apostolic drive, shutting it up within the narrowness of a lifeless asceticism or a paralysing legalism.

She began by freeing herself from the direction of the priest Don Luigi Cogrossi, who had been instrumental in choosing that city as the cradle of the planned Institute. Rosa soon realised that he was not the right man to guide the foundation, and she firmly set him aside.

Then came the providential meeting with Fr. Tornatore, a priest of the Mission. Mother Rosa saw in him the man the Lord was sending to guide her and stand beside her in those beginnings; she entrusted herself to him without reserve and was drawn by his personal piety, for besides being known for his learning as a professor at the famous Alberoni College, he was regarded by many as a holy man.

The foundress not only agreed to change the Institute's name, as already mentioned, following her own vision of Mother Saint Anne, but she would have liked Fr. Tornatore to be recognised as "first father" and founder, which, it seems, corresponded to his own inner aspiration (49). Indeed, he would always regard the Daughters of Saint Anne as his daughters.

Her liberation from Fr. Tornatore's influence was gradual but complete. The first step was the separation of the internal and external forum; Mother Rosa, as we have seen, broke off spiritual direction with him quite early and eventually confession as well. We think it was not easy for the cofounder's spirituality to harmonise with that of the foundress, by now enriched by intense infused experience and open to the great biblical and ecclesial horizons. Yet she wanted him beside her in everything concerning the running of the Institute; indeed, she had the diocesan bishop appoint him ecclesiastical superior and asked the superior general of his congregation to free him from other commitments so that he could give himself fully to the Work (cf. FIOCCHI, I, pp. 222-241).

Even in those beginnings there were differing views on the direction the Institute should take. For example, when it came to accepting the hospital in Cento, while Don Luigi Cogrossi still had the direction, Fr. Tornatore advised against it because of the ambiguity he saw in that foundation, since Fr. Giambattista Tagiasco, who had requested the sisters, wanted them to appear not as religious but as lay nurses (50). The foundress decided on that foundation because it fully matched her experience of this form of apostolic charity, but she insisted that the nursing sisters' presence as religious be respected. Interestingly, to make sure this was God's will, Mother Rosa turned to her former director Don Firpo, from whom she had earlier parted (cf. FIOCCHI, I, p. 173f).

But the decisive moment of liberation from dependence on the cofounder came in 1872, by drastic imposition of the Holy See.

In June she had presented, together with him, the text of the Rules to Pope Pius IX. They had been drawn up by the priest in the form of a dialogue between Saint Anne and her daughters, in a style and approach the consultors found unsuitable, and they voted against it; indeed, the text was passed on to the Holy Office and, after a long wait, the order came to burn all the already printed copies of the Rules and to remove Fr. Tornatore, who was absolutely forbidden to concern himself with the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Certainly, people opposed to Fr. Tornatore played a part in the affair of the Rules. Be that as it may, it was clear that Rome wished to protect the Institute and the foundress herself from a direction it judged unsuitable.

In the pages of her diary Mother Rosa poured out the atrocious sufferings of that spring of 1872. She was convinced that the Rules had been written by the Father under God's inspiration; in them she had found formulated, in substance, the ideal and spirit of God's Work according to the light she herself had received. In Vatican circles, however, she found only prejudice, humiliating mockery and incomprehension. With no one to consult, abandoned by God in darkness and aridity, she had moments when she saw herself "led to the brink of despair" (M 3, p. 13f).

She understood everything when she had the consolation of being received by Pius IX and heard from his lips: "I want this rule to be drawn up by you alone." She tells it herself, and adds:

"Then he went on to tell me to leave that priest, that is, T.; that it was better, because I would at last enjoy peace and would no longer have to suffer so much... I thought: Who can have told him of the sufferings he said I endured because of Mr. T.? It was true! But I had never told anyone what I was going through so painfully" (M 2, pp. 68-71; 5, pp. 59-76).

Her humility and, in part, that mysterious bond which suffering itself had created between her and the cofounder kept her from understanding that the Roman Curia's distrust of the priest was matched by its trust in her charism as foundress. Even so, the process was not easy. A first draft she made herself was not accepted. She had to resign herself to leaving the work in the hands of some religious appointed by the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars; but she reacted strongly on learning that they meant to give the Daughters of Saint Anne a legislation modeled on the constitutions of other institutes.

On a new journey to Rome she defended the distinctive character of God's Work and obtained recognition of her right to take part directly in the drafting. Thus a text, once again drawn up by Fr. Tornatore, was approved ad experimentum by decree of Cardinal Vannicelli, protector of the Institute, on June 12, 1874.

The next protector, Cardinal Giuseppe Berardi, ordered Fr. Tornatore to write the Rules to be submitted to the Congregation, since no one was managing to do so and Mother Rosa had also rejected the text written by the consultor Fr. Bianchi. The new text was submitted in January or February 1876, and in April the Institute received the decree of praise. Fr. Tornatore's autograph manuscript is kept at the Congregation for Religious. The text underwent successive changes by the Congregation of Bishops and Religious and was definitively approved in 1892.

After some time, at the foundress's request, the Holy See authorised the cofounder to resume his office as ecclesiastical superior of the Institute and to take part in its direction. Indeed, the circulars sent from time to time to the communities, although very often signed by Mother Rosa as well, were written by Fr. Tornatore until 1888.

The foundress, however, preferred to depend ever more directly on the Congregation of Bishops and Regulars, through the Cardinal protector, especially after the Institute's pontifical approval (April 21, 1879). And it was the Cardinal prefect of that same Congregation who urged her to move the Generalate to Rome to free her from the influences and constraints of Piacenza, especially after what happened at the general chapter of 1881.

She felt herself ever more guided by God, free from the interference of anyone who did not live the Work from within. She wrote in September 1887:

"O my Love! How well you maintain and direct your Institute!... It needs no direction. Now I understand certain things that sometimes made me afraid, but now that nothing is hidden from me any longer, I calmly let everything take its course, thinking that my Good orders it all. Most holy Mary, my Mother! what a sweet thought it is to know that my Good himself sees to providing the right people for his Work! The work my poor head does is because he allows his slave to contribute her material effort too, so as to make the work complete" (M 5.5, p. 74f).

Precisely at that time Mother Rosa was enduring a bitter battle waged by Fr. Tornatore, by word and in writing, even pestering prelates and cardinals, to assert what he considered his rights over the direction of the Institute. Her letters of 1887 and 1888 to Bishop Granito di Belmonte reflect the bitterness caused by this tiresome harassment (51).

After the general chapter of 1888, at which he was excluded, the Institute's general government did without Fr. Tornatore entirely. He, however, continued to love it as his own work and to feel spiritually united with the Daughters of Saint Anne. Even after his death on January 31, 1895, he was, one may say, officially ignored, until the Special Chapter of 1969-71 chose to rehabilitate him, recognising him as Cofounder in the full sense. On July 9, 1981, in a rite presided over by the Bishop of Piacenza, Enrico Manfredini, his remains were transferred to the Motherhouse (52).

Mother Rosa, who at the time of that 1888 chapter and again in 1896 had "the temptation to resign" (M 9.6, p. 12f), continued to feel herself a useless instrument of God's Work, yet directed it with a sure hand together with her collaborators in the general government, with Bishop Granito di Belmonte as external adviser and the Cardinal Protector as her support in relations with the Apostolic See.

2. Spiritual guide and caring mother.

We already know of the foundress's motherly affection for the spiritual daughters God had given her. Her sense of responsibility before the One who called them and entrusted them to her care gives her love a sense of presence among them, joined to a keen pastoral awareness that makes her wholly attentive to their good.

Her letters to superiors and to individual sisters testify to her delicate, almost meticulous motherly attentions, both to their bodily health and to the interests of the spirit. To express how close she feels to each one she uses terms full of spontaneous warmth:

"I keep you with me... everywhere I go"

- "I feel all the troubles you have, and I asked the Lord to transfer them onto my shoulders, for my heart already shares the pain"

- "I keep you close at my right hand, and every morning I commend you to God, my only All"

- "You are closer to me than if I had you at my side..."

- "I always pray, and I can say in all truth that not a morning passes that I leave church without praying for all of you in particular." (53).

She shares not only the worries and ups and downs of the good religious, who console her heart, but also the situations and struggles of those in danger of being unfaithful to their commitments; she prays for them and offers her penances for them. She writes on September 19, 1892:

"I had promised to scourge myself to the point of blood if my Good granted me the conversion of a Daughter of Saint Anne who was in great danger of losing her vocation... I saw her free and wholly returned to Jesus" (M 12.2, p. 5f).

With her feminine sense of detail she keeps every particular of each house in mind. In a letter to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, superior of the Piacenza house, she asks:

"How are the flowers doing? Have the trees taken? The portress's ones must be lovely: tell her I was very pleased with her work and that the Holy Mother will keep her alive for many years, and that she should not overtire herself" (L 2-3-1872).

But that same pastoral care involves vigilance, which knows how to forestall human weaknesses, and timely correction as well. Mother Rosa did not hesitate to use this means whenever necessary. Sr. A. Santina Solenghi testifies at the Process:

"I always noticed her prudence in the reprimands she gave us, in which she was severe, yes, but she had a certain something that made one submit to her. Then when she saw that the sister was sorry, she treated her gently and encouraged her" (Summ., p. 292f).

She was least indulgent precisely with those she knew were most attached to her, as appears in her letters to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa and Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni, both superiors. For the more important interventions she prepared herself with prayer and penance. In August 1885, during the sisters' spiritual exercises, she noticed that the sermons were bearing no fruit in them, because "their hearts were soaked in worldly things." She prayed and took the discipline. Finally, on the feast of the Assumption, she felt moved to intervene:

"Well, this evening this donkey was able to speak, and yes, they have already come to tell me frankly that they learned nothing from the holy exercises, but that the last word I said to them, oh! all of them, throwing themselves at my feet, ask forgiveness and want to change. God has shown them mercy, what goodness!" (M 5.4, p. 62f).

It was above all during her visits to the communities, in personal dialogue with individual sisters, that she knew how to combine reprimands with motherly care. Reading the notes she jotted down rapidly, in broken phrases, one is left with a rather negative impression of the sisters' spiritual and even moral level. She uncovers not only common faults but serious abuses, hidden intentions, concealment and pretense on the part of superiors... Often her only comment is: Horror! (cf. M fasc. 6, 7 and 8). Perhaps this pessimistic stance should be attributed to her innate insight into people's inner lives as well as to her tendency to see things darkly, which she herself acknowledged, as mentioned elsewhere.

In the annual circulars to the whole Institute, alongside reasons for encouragement at the growing vitality and development of God's Work, there are also negative observations and laments from her grieving heart over failures of observance and other "black spots" that sadden Mother Saint Anne.

Much as she liked to receive information directly from the sisters themselves, she loathed accusations and gossip that could harm someone's reputation or disturb the peace of the community (L to Bishop Granito di Belmonte: 30-7-1896).

For Mother Rosa, personally visiting the houses and meeting the superiors and individual sisters was the primary duty of her service as superior general. To bring her daughters the comfort of her presence she faced the hardships of long journeys and the discomfort of her illnesses. Her secretary, Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, testified at the Process:

"From the very beginning of the Institute's foundation I learned from other sisters that she visited the houses very often and was always here and there, so much so that once, when asked where she lived, she replied jokingly: On the railways! To visit the houses she did not shrink from hardships and sacrifices" (Summ., p. 329).

But there was also that other, no less important, form of encounter: an unceasing correspondence that took up entire days, to the point of giving the impression, contrary to the truth, that she governed centrally from behind a desk. The night for God in unitive contemplation, the day also for God, but busy with his Work. There was no room for idleness.

"The sin of idleness I do not have," she wrote to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, "perhaps the only one I will not find at God's judgment seat, since I have committed every other one" (L 15-10-1871).

Returning from her journeys she would find mountains of letters, all of which she felt obliged to answer, which was impossible without her secretaries' help. But the sisters were used to letters written in her own hand; through the strokes of her handwriting and her incisive phrases they seemed to feel the beating of her mother's heart. At times they complained of the impersonal letters written at her orders (cf. L to Sr. A. Gaudenzia Martinelli: 15-6-1880).

She experiences special divine help in her heavy work, especially when spiritual aridity and other sufferings are added to fatigue.

"Dear Monsignor: Trials come day after day, they never stop, never! each more terrible than the last. I feel crushed and see my poor body too worn down: the years, the constant journeys, the sufferings and above all the terrible torment of my poor spirit, tossed about on every side. I do not know how or where to find calm. Work! I feel a duty of conscience driving me; my human nature shrinks from work, it seems to have lost my energy..."

- "After long suffering I resolved to set out and take up my old life: better to die working than to surrender to the cure!" (L to Bishop Granito di Belmonte: 18-6-1888, 2-9-1893).

She expresses the same indomitable will to die under the burden of her mission as foundress in a fine paragraph of the circular of 7-12-1895:

"If nothing so far has been able to halt my steps for your good and for the greater glory of God, I assure you that, until the last breath of my life, I will always be the same and will not fail to come to your aid in any need of yours."

In Mother Rosa's Memoirs one frequently finds her lived experience of divine help through the charismatic gift of insight into people's situations and through signs by which God lets her know what is happening in this or that community, what is troubling this or that sister. These are almost always painful situations that make her suffer and turn to prayer, redoubling her penances. Very often she feels that a higher light suggests what she should decide in certain difficult cases concerning the Work (cf. M 4.2, p. 81-84). She writes on February 23, 1875:

"When I have to speak about certain small matters, I seem to find them all easily in my mind, and other serious matters of the Work so clear in my mind, as if I only had to bring them out ready-made. Oh! how often I think that I have not had the least thought of my own in this Work and have only had the material task of putting in place what my Good keeps teaching me!" (M 4.3, p. 28).

3. The art of sharing the responsibility of government.

It has often been observed that charismatic superiors tend to be accused of authoritarianism, certainly not from ambition for power, but from the habit of feeling enlightened and guided by God, with the risk of not giving due weight to others' opinions and proposals. Inside and outside the Institute there were people who disagreed with the way of centralising everything in her own person that was attributed to the foundress. One of the most delicate moments in relations with the Holy See came when the order to set up a general council, as existed in all institutes of pontifical right, was not obeyed. Mother Rosa asked forgiveness and humbly obeyed. There was, however, a reason of evangelical charity that led her not to inform even her own collaborators of matters concerning individual sisters: the sisters' right to the secrecy a superior must keep regarding what she learns by virtue of her office. In 1880 she left a written account of an interesting reaction of hers:

"I received a gentle rebuke from the Lord, who asked me why I had slightly given up keeping everything silent, even the smallest matters of the Work, for I never used to say anything and this was very pleasing to the Lord, whereas I had to do myself great violence to say anything (I mean matters of the Work, not matters about myself, no, oh! never those!).

But since the Protector accused me of being too secretive and said this was not right, that in this way the poor sisters would never learn anything, and that I was obliged to tell those close to me what was going on, so as to instruct them better and tell them how I went about removing whatever abuse or imperfection or other thing occurred: so, although I did it reluctantly, I did it, I can say, by force of obedience.

Oh! when I heard this rebuke, it was very dear to me, because nothing is needed to put it into practice. So I can say I have closed the door, and that is the end of it. Yes, my Good, I will speak no more. And to tell the truth, besides feeling reluctant, I also saw that I gained nothing good by it, quite the opposite, it brought ill feeling. In the past I had always refrained, and so everyone thought well of the Daughters of Saint Anne, even though one or more of them made me their target. Oh! my silence did good all the same, it caused no unpleasantness (?), no one knew anything, everything stayed with me" (M 4.5, pp. 187-189).

Mother Rosa was convinced that the good running of the Institute depends above all on the careful choice of superiors and on their responsible care for the good of the sisters. Of course, the Work's rapid growth, with houses multiplying in Italy, America and Africa, made it difficult to find suitable leaders for every community. From her correspondence with them and above all from her circulars, often very harsh, one gathers that not all were equal to the task entrusted to them. The foundress feels it her duty to denounce with blunt frankness the unevangelical conduct of superiors, but also to form them and guide them in the right way of governing. Besides her correspondence with each of them, she uses the circulars mentioned and especially conferences during her visits, gathering them by region, and the general chapters, which are usually preceded by a retreat.

She has an ideal image of the superior, whose features she tries to instill at every opportunity. First of all, she bitterly condemns the ambition to become superior, "an accursed vice that reigns in the Institute," as well as "the pride, vanity and vainglory" that dominate many, as she has seen in her visits; she prays the Lord to give her back "daughters full of his love, humble, ready to accept any office, from superior to laundress, from superior to cook" (L Circ. 15-6-1894).

A superior's first task is to be guide and support to her sisters in fidelity to their vocation, knowing that superiors "will have to render an account to God for their souls" (L Circ. 1890, 20-1-1892). But she cannot be an effective guide unless she herself is a model and example for them:

"Superiors are the shadow of the other religious, who all run after it and go as the shadow shows them the way" (L to Sr. Francesca Camisa: 13-5-1872)

- "The superior must be the lighthouse that guides everyone to a safe harbour... Look after the interests of your heavenly Spouse, win souls for him. Courage, then, and holy rivalry with your beloved sisters in advancing in virtue!" (L to Sr. A. Gerarda Canovi: 30-4-1900)

- "Superiors are the candlesticks: as their flame burns, the others entrusted to them catch fire in turn and, true torches burning with sacrifice and love, seek to be consumed in the burning Heart of Jesus" (L Circ.: 3-3-1897).

The superior must be the first in observing the Rules and in punctuality at community exercises. Her presence in the household tasks and her participation in fraternal recreation also contribute to a good atmosphere in the community. She wrote to one of them in these terms:

"One does not go to recreation thinking it is something meant for the scatterbrained but not for oneself; that is how stupid eccentricities arise. Go to recreation, humble yourselves, you proud ones, talk with your sisters..." (L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 25-8-1869).

The virtues she most wishes to see in superiors are "charity, prudence, humility and patience" (L to Sr. A. Del Tabor Saldini: 28-4-1900; to Sr. A. Agnese Facchini: 29-4-1900). She insists especially on gentleness, avoiding all harshness in correction. Indeed, the art of correcting at the right time and in the right way, without losing one's temper, without humiliating, with the sole aim of doing good to the sister at fault or simply careless, is not easy. In her letters Mother Rosa gives serious warnings to superiors who are harsh or let themselves be carried away by their first impulse in correcting, and adds very wise advice on how to carry out this pastoral duty (cf. L to Sr. A. Adelaide Pezzoni: 1871 (or 1869); to Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: 10-7-1885, 29-12-1885).

If it is true that the foundress had reasons for personally exercising the general government of the Institute all her life, assisted by her most faithful secretaries, it is equally true that she respected on principle the responsibility of local and regional superiors, giving them the fullest trust in the decisions and initiatives they were to take. Indeed, she encouraged them to act on mature personal choices after taking counsel. She wrote to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, who was too used to turning to her dear Mother for everything:

"My dear daughter, try to be more self-assured...; in certain cases you must make your own decisions: first commend yourself to God, and then forward, with courage!" (L 27-8-1872).

In her letters to other superiors we find similar words of trust in whatever they decide for themselves:

"You did everything well, I approve all you do, go forward with courage!"

- "When I receive your letters and see that you do and act as God inspires you, they bring me immense consolation. Courage!"

- "I would not know what to tell you: commend yourself to Saint Anne and then do what you feel inspired to do"

- "I want you to take this as advice and not as a command: you are closer and can see things in a better light"

- "I leave you completely free to do what you think best"

- "All you have done is very good; indeed, always do the same, because you know the needs of the house"

- "What do you think? I await your approval"

- "Be cheerful! and the sisters too. Do not worry, for Jesus is thinking of you: you think of him, and he thinks of you"

- "You did very well..., do not worry; I approve what you have done and will do"

- "I leave everything to your wisdom and will always approve whatever you do, knowing how much the good of the Institute means to you"

- "I know you do better than any advice, courage!"

- "In everything I tell you that you are doing well and I am pleased."

What kept the sisters from acting with freedom of spirit in their responsibilities was, besides some sisters' lack of self-confidence, the fear of not looking good in the eyes of the foundress, who was known to be aware of whatever happened in every house. This constant flow of information made certain superiors uneasy, and they tried to hinder free communication between their sisters and the superior general; in her circulars she repeatedly denounces this violation of rights, which springs from "the fear that the sisters will write to Mother about them: this fear is born of duplicity" (L Circ: 31-1-1880).

"You harm yourselves both with regard to us and with regard to your sisters, because you give us reason to suspect that you are doing things contrary to your duty, and you give your sisters reason to think you are not in harmony with us. How different is the community where the sisters and the superior are in good harmony with us! I can assure you that the superior is loved and respected; thoughts in that community are in accord; there is no grumbling, there are no subterfuges, and the Lord's peace enables them to overcome every sacrifice" (L Circ.: 2-3-1895).

From experience of the content of many letters that reached her by that route, however, she knew that very often they were inspired by resentment or personal interest; in them one could hear "the perfect sound of grumbling" (L to Bishop Granito di Belmonte: 13-8-1890).

Although her first concern was to train superiors in the art of governing well, since where government is good obedience is usually good, she did not fail to instill in all the Daughters of Saint Anne the life of obedience, which "is the pivot of true holiness" (L Circ: 1-1-1889).

"Obey if you want to be saints," she repeated in the communities (L to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 4-5-1869).

"On the road to paradise is written: Obedience" (M 4.4, p. 14).

She taught the sisters to "see in their superiors the person of dear Jesus, and not to be demanding in wanting the superior to be perfect in everything" (L Circ: 1890).

4. Formation: criteria and methods.

Too rapid growth in a new institute risks producing a leafy tree that shoots up into the air but lacks deep roots. More than once Mother Rosa had to hear such a judgment on the Daughters of Saint Anne from people of standing, as appears in her book:

"One of the shepherds said to me in an irritated tone:

- I tell you that your way of proceeding has little foundation... You are going too fast in the work you do: you need a brake, otherwise these labourers will achieve nothing good...

He went on ironically:

- Let me tell you that I compare these fields to the pumpkin plant, which spreads and is all leaves; in the end its fruit is a pumpkin!

Then I answered him:

- The time will come when this pumpkin will harden and give you indigestion! It will rise above all the plants and finally spread its branches from pole to pole; its roots will suffer no harm..., its fruits will be tasty to the Bride of my Lord and its flowers will have a fragrance all their own..." (TC, p. 274f).

She understood from the start that the way to make "the pumpkin harden" was the solid formation of the Daughters of Saint Anne. She was aware of so serious a responsibility and trembled at the thought of having to render an account to God for so many souls entrusted to her direction: "How will I fare before God's judgment seat?" (M 3, p. 71).

She was especially gifted as a spiritual guide and had an influence over the sisters that ensured a favourable reception of her teachings and demands. What she lacked in human learning and pedagogical training was amply made up for by her intuition, guided by light from above, and by her experience. Judging from the letters, a good number of sisters, especially those of the first generation she formed personally in Piacenza, continued to receive genuine spiritual direction from their Mother, in which affectionate encouragement alternated with the sternest reproofs.

But she was not content with this personal guidance. She was diligent about instructions to the community; "every Sunday she called together all the religious of the community to exhort them on their religious duties" (Summ. p. 56).

"Besides the conferences Mr. Tornatore often gave, and besides the retreats she had preached to them, she often invited some religious to preach" (Summ., p. 259). Mention was made above of her conferences, even real series of formative conferences, which she prepared carefully and of which many outlines survive, as well as verbatim transcripts made by her secretaries; many of them concern very concrete details of a Daughter of Saint Anne's conduct both in community life and outside the house.

She attached great importance to the influence, positive or negative, that confessors and spiritual directors could have on the sisters' formation. She complains of certain directors who are too quick to believe in the extraordinary graces some sisters claim to have received from God, having them write them down, etc.; the result is that "their imaginations become overexcited" (M 5.3, p. 30f; 5.4, p. 23; 5.5, pp. 15-19; 9.1, pp. 18-20). Worst of all was when they tried to make the sisters lose confidence in the foundress:

"Certain shepherds were so incapable of giving true and sound direction to those dear labourers that they caused me much grief. Moreover, they thought they could manage to put me out of the field so as to overturn that fine cultivation all over again" (TC, p. 270f).

In the circulars superiors are reminded of their obligation to find suitable priests for conferences to the community, especially for the annual retreat. She was demanding in choosing such ministers of the Word, especially when the Institute's spirit might suffer. In 1892 she asked Bishop Granito di Belmonte for "a good and holy priest" to preach the retreat to the sisters; but fearing that the one designated was a well-known priest, she ruled him out: "I would not want it to be him: no, no! He does not know our spirit, he is not at all for the Daughters of Saint Anne. He may be a saint, but of another spirit and not ours. Is that understood?" (L 18-8-1892).

She urged on superiors not only the means of spiritual and moral formation but also those suited to intellectual and technical instruction. She wanted every community to have a small library, stocked above all with spiritual books (cf. L to Sr. A. Andila Briccoli: 11-4-1895).

But her most attentive care was for the formation of young candidates. Witnesses at the informative process note the seriousness with which the foundress proceeded in admitting postulants, unhesitatingly excluding those she saw were unsuitable (Summ., pp. 14, 521, 648).

She attached no importance, however, to whether a candidate could bring a dowry, if she showed a good vocation. Those who during the postulancy behaved in a way that cast doubt on the sincerity of their vocation she ordered to be dismissed as soon as possible (cf. L to Sr. A. Paola Bueciotti: 20-5-1872; to Sr. A. Francesca Camisa: 5-9-1872; to Sr. A. Francesca Savignoni: 13-3-1880; to Sr. A. Gaudenzia Martinelli: 6-4-1885).

The novitiate, a time of more intense formation and experience of consecrated life, was a special object of her care. Not content with entrusting the novices to a suitable mistress, she looked after them personally through her conferences. Twenty-three of these instructions survive, along with several outlines of others given to the novices on various dates. In general they contain a first part of an ascetical nature and then what she calls "religious etiquette," that is, practical advice on social and religious courtesy, personal hygiene, self-control, etc., all drawn from commentary on the Rules (M 10.2, 10.3).

In the early days of the foundation, the young sisters were sent after six months of novitiate to houses with urgent needs, especially in times of epidemic (Summ., p. 522). Later she preferred that they begin the novitiate "after testing them in the work of holy charity in caring for the sick" (M 5.5, p. 6f).

Formation did not end with the novitiate or with the period of temporary vows. What we might call "ongoing formation" was entrusted to each superior and, at the level of the Institute, provided by the foundress herself, for some years with Fr. Tornatore's collaboration, through the circular letters, as mentioned above. The goal of such formation was the holiness of every Daughter of Saint Anne.

"May the Lord make you saints, and great saints," she repeats in her letters. She wrote to Sr. A. Celsa Speranza:

"Tell me, do you believe I want only one thing: your sanctification? Yes, it is true. Well then, great wretch that I am, I never cease asking my God to sanctify you all through the merits of my dear Crucified. When I clasp myself to him in my poor room, oh! how strongly I clasp you to his Heart! O sweet Love! Yes, my dear daughter, look for me in him, and I promise you will always find me" (L undated, no. 76).

In the Memoirs we find pleas like this: "I would like them all to be after your own Heart, my Love!" (M 11.2, p. 82f). And in a circular of 1893: "We greatly desire to see you all after God's own heart" (L Circ: 23-4-1893). And as a sure means of walking according to God's will and attaining holiness in the life they have embraced, she insists on observance of the Rules, "the pivot that holds the wheel steady and makes it run true" (L Circ: 20-2-1893).

5. The "Sons of Saint Anne": an idealistic project that failed.

Mother Rosa speaks of founding the Sons of Saint Anne as early as 1882: a men's institute to stand alongside the Daughters of Saint Anne, forming with them and with the Tertiaries of Saint Anne already mentioned (54) the three Orders, symbolised by the three drops of blood she had been shown in a vision. In September of that year she had been encouraged by "a learned and holy Franciscan" to undertake that foundation in earnest (M 5.1, pp. 89-94; 5.2, p. 62f, 66f, 105f).

And it was precisely her desire to provide suitably and stably for the formation of the Daughters of Saint Anne according to the spirit of the Institute that drove her to such a work.

"How clearly I see the need to have the Sons of Saint Anne! What pain I feel seeing these poor creatures guided by different spirits, for one inclines towards recollection while another, too lax, slackens the reins and they find themselves dissipated. And that inner voice: Set your hand to the work: they will help you!... But I feel an enormous reluctance, so that I do not even know how to think about it; it is so strong that it overcomes me. My Love, I will wait for obedience and submit everything to it" (M 5.1, pp. 29f, 58, 60; 5.5, p. 5).

The project took shape in 1886: Don Gennaro Granito di Belmonte, received in private audience by Pope Leo XIII on December 6, 1886, explained his intentions orally. The Pontiff invited him to summarise his ideas in writing, which he did on December 8, entrusting the document to Mons. Marzolini, who was very close to the Pope; receiving no direct reply, he pressed the same Monsignor, and the Pontiff, through the same channel, made his will known: he was to begin the work in Naples under the Archbishop's direction and then, with the Archbishop's recommendation, seek pontifical approval. Don Gennaro then asked Cardinal Sanfelice for permission to begin the work (L January 6, 1887), explaining the steps already taken. A few days later, on January 10, the Cardinal replied: non expedire.

When the "Sons of Saint Anne" project failed, the following year, 1888, Don Gennaro thought he would please Mother Rosa and benefit himself and other priests by gathering those priests who were already ministering in the sisters' houses into a Devout League of priests for the good of the Daughters of Saint Anne. Without consulting Mother Rosa further about its form (L 16-5-1888, end of May 1888; M 9.4, p. 13f), he presented the project to the Archbishop of Naples on August 26, and Cardinal Sanfelice approved the work on August 28. Don Gennaro informed Mother Rosa (the letter, unfortunately, has been lost), and the Foundress, fearing that these priests would go to the sisters' houses to preach retreats without any further formation or preparation, gave a flat no to the idea (L 31-8-1888). Then she wrote in her diary:

"The work begun of the Sons of Saint Anne grieves me greatly, because I see it is not as God desires. Instead it seems to me a wish to take on too much of the direction of the Daughters of Saint Anne without first being thoroughly at one with the Work and seeking its true spirit, besides not knowing what our Constitutions and customs are; moreover, they think too soon that they are capable of directing. After 22 years of continual struggles and of studying the sisters' character and the situation they are in!...

Oh! if only I could explain the wound I received when it was announced to me! Oh! what I felt on hearing that, without any agreement, everything is being done and ordered as if they were our superiors! What pain I felt on hearing that they would go to preach in the houses! My God! what will happen? All this without my knowing anything. I see and feel that Jesus is not pleased..." (M 9.5, pp. 87-91).

Faced with Mother Rosa's strong reaction, Don Gennaro defended himself in a letter to Cardinal Alimonda (5-9-1888), explaining that these priests would be only "most humble servants of the Daughters of Saint Anne" and would have "no interference or jurisdiction over the sisters." In any case, the Devout League came to nothing.

So the project of a men's branch came to nothing. Mother Rosa resigned herself to the failure, convinced that a foundation conceived in that way, as purely external, paternalistic help, was of no use and would indeed have been harmful to the Daughters of Saint Anne.

At the end of my work, after classifying and weaving together hundreds of pieces of information drawn chiefly from Mother Rosa's Memoirs and letters, I am still left with a pile of unused notes, although they contain information and ideas that could enrich some of the aspects already presented of the Servant of God's profile and provide material for other chapters on the various evangelical virtues, such as poverty, humility, chastity, temperance... But in a synthesis such as the one entrusted to me, it is not a matter of exhausting the research - think of the more than nine thousand letters - nor of filling in every detail. Anyone who wishes to know how Mother Rosa practiced each of the virtues to a heroic degree may consult the Positio super virtutibus, which will be printed by the Congregation for the Causes of Saints.

I hope that the seven chapters, which I have prepared with care and affection, are enough to outline in its full dimension the genuinely Christian and truly exceptional personality of Rosa Gattorno, and to set before the Daughters of Saint Anne the great model of experience of God and active charity they have in their spiritual Mother.
